2.1. Elementary sets Definition 2.1.1 (Elementary set). A set is elementary if it is a finite union of boxes. Every box is elementary, since a box is a union of one box. The empty set is elementary as well. Theorem 2.1.2 (Boolean closure). If E and F are elementary sets, then so are their union and their difference, by regrouping boxes. Proof. Write each set as a finite union of boxes and combine. The union of two finite unions is finite. Exercise 2.1.3. Show that the intersection of two elementary sets is elementary; that is, the family is closed under intersection. Deduce the same for the difference of two elementary sets. 4 2.1. Elementary sets without appealing to any choice principle. Deduce that the elementary sets form a Boolean algebra. Remark 2.1.4. The Boolean algebra generated by the boxes is the collection of elementary sets. This observation is used throughout these notes. Lemma 2.1.5. Every elementary set has a well-defined volume. The volume is additive on disjoint unions. Proof. Decompose the set into disjoint boxes and add volumes. The result does not depend on the decomposition chosen. Example 2.1.6. The union of two intervals and their endpoints is elementary, as each interval is a box in one dimension. 5 2.1. Elementary sets and the finite union of boxes is elementary by definition. Proof. This line is prose and ends no item of an unproved kind. The decomposition is immediate. 2.2. Finite unions Definition 2.2.1 (Finite union). A finite union of elementary sets is again elementary. 6
